title: Atlantic Highly Migratory Species; Atlantic Bluefin Tuna Fisheries; Closure of the General Category October Through November Fishery for 2025
summary:
The federal government announced two moves: tighter U.S. export controls on two overseas companies, and a temporary pause on part of the Atlantic bluefin tuna commercial fishery for the rest of October and November 2025.

On trade, the Commerce Department is adding two firms—Yant Insaat in Turkey and Royal Impact Trading LLC in the United Arab Emirates—to a list that triggers strict U.S. export restrictions. Any shipment to them now needs a government license, which the agency says it will generally deny. This is meant to protect U.S. national and economic security by blocking sensitive goods from reaching risky end users. It could benefit companies that compete with these firms and those focused on compliance and risk management. On the flip side, the listed companies and their business partners will face disrupted supply chains, and U.S. exporters connected to them may lose sales or need to quickly adjust contracts and screening processes.

On fisheries, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is closing the Atlantic bluefin tuna “General” commercial fishery for large fish for the rest of October and November, with an automatic reopening on December 1. The agency cites strong catch rates this year, previous overages, and the need to stay within international limits to avoid even larger paybacks next year. During the closure, tag-and-release fishing is allowed, but keeping large bluefin is not. This action aims to protect the stock and keep the United States in line with international commitments, which supports long-term sustainability and future fishing opportunities. It benefits the resource, science-based management, and businesses that depend on a healthy fishery over time. Those most affected in the near term are commercial fishermen and dealers who rely on late-season landings, as well as coastal communities tied to that income. The agency signaled it will keep monitoring conditions and could adjust if new opportunities arise, while reminding industry of timely catch reporting to guide any next steps.

Overall, both decisions prioritize security and sustainability, with near-term costs for some businesses and fishermen to help avoid larger risks down the road.
